CHAPTER III · THE CHURCH IN ACTS
Men and brethren, this scripture must needs have been fulfilled, which the Holy Ghost by the mouth of David spake before concerning Judas, which was guide to them that took Jesus.
Peter tells the believers that Judas “was guide to them that took Jesus”, and that he “was numbered with us, and had obtained part of this ministry”.
That he may take part of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place.
The apostles pray for a man to take the place “from which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place”.
Tradition, by who said it and when · 1 source
What Scripture says of his end

Matthew: when Judas saw that Jesus “was condemned”, he “repented himself”, brought back the thirty pieces of silver and said, “I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood”. He “cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.”
Matthew: the chief priests would not put “the price of blood” into the treasury. They “bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in”, and so it was called “The field of blood”.

Acts, in Peter's words: “this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out.” The field was called “Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood.”

Each account quotes Scripture: Matthew the words “spoken by Jeremy the prophet” about the thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field; Acts two Psalms, “Let his habitation be desolate” and “his bishoprick let another take”.

The two accounts stand side by side here and are not merged. They differ on who bought the field (the chief priests in Matthew, Judas himself in Acts) and on how he died (he “hanged himself” in Matthew; “falling headlong, he burst asunder” in Acts). Mark, Luke and John say nothing of his death.
c. 70 First reported by Papias, fragment 3, preserved by Oecumenius Later tradition

How did Judas die? Matthew and Acts tell it differently. (Harmonising views first, as Strauss lists them, then the view that they differ.)
He hanged himself, then the body fell and burst

Easton (1897), quoting an earlier writer; Casaubon, Kuinoel, Winer and others, as listed by Strauss (1846); the Latin Vulgate's wording of Acts 1:18, “when he had hanged himself”, as reported by Kerr (ISBE, 1915)
Easton: the rope gave way or the branch broke, and he fell headlong and was crushed. Acts tells the end of what Matthew begins.
Scholars Matthew 27:5·Acts 1:18 M. G. Easton, 1897·D. F. Strauss (trans. George Eliot), 1846·C. M. Kerr, 1915
“Hanged himself” means he was choked, and then fell
Matthew Henry (early 18th century), following Henry Hammond
Henry takes Matthew's word to mean that Judas was “strangled, or choked with grief and horror”, after which he fell headlong and burst.
He survived the hanging and died later
Oecumenius and other ancient commentators, as reported by Strauss (1846)
On this view Matthew tells of a failed attempt, and Acts of the death that came afterwards.
Scholars D. F. Strauss (trans. George Eliot), 1846
D. F. Strauss (1846), with K. Hase
Strauss argues that each writer knew only the story he tells, since otherwise he could not have left out the other half, and judges the attempts to reconcile them a failure.
